newsitem.title: CONGO: French leave Congo foes to observe new truce alone.
newsitem.headline: French leave Congo foes to observe new truce alone.

text.p: Congo's rival factions agreed to extend a truce but were left alone to make it stick after France pulled its forces from the capital Brazzaville earlier than announced.
"The chiefs of staff (of both sides) have agreed to prolong the cease-fire for a period of seven days starting tonight at midnight (2300 GMT)," they said in a joint statement on Friday.

A spokesman for Bernard Kolelas, the city's mayor who has been mediating between President Pascal Lissouba and his rival and predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso, said the deal was made in a national mediation commission chaired by Kolelas.

Fighting between the forces of Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso flared in the capital on June 5, killing hundreds of people and prompting France to mount a military operation to evacuate several thousand foreigners.
A three-day truce agreed in talks at the French embassy stopped the clashes on Wednesday, but the new extension was agreed without French involvement, officials said.
Ignoring a U.N. plea for them to stay, the 1,250 French troops completed their pullout on Friday, flying out of the airport and leaving the warring sides to their own devices.
"The last soldiers left today," French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the one remaining Western envoy, told Reuters by telephone.
"That leaves 30 gendarmes who are staying to protect the diplomats, that is myself and 12 colleagues."

Earlier, an international Red Cross team took 60 children from an orphanage in the no man's land around the airport to safety in Bacongo, a southern suburb held by Kolelas' neutral militia to which thousands of residents have fled.
The new truce was a positive sign amid widespread fears that fighting could resume after the French departure.

U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who with African mediators has called on the Security Council to send an African intervention force to "Brazza", repeatedly urged Paris to keep at least some troops in position until such a force arrived.
Despite the withdrawal, Paris has not ruled out playing a future role in peace efforts in its old colony.

Congo's trouble began when Lissouba, a friend of recently ousted Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, tried to disarm the militia of Marxist-turned-capitalist Sassou Nguesso, whom he had succeeded as president in 1992 elections.
The foes were, along with Kolelas, front-runners in presidential elections due in late July and now postponed.
